stem: Which of the following is a common **cause of business failure**?

options.content: Running out of cash to pay its bills on time
options.rationale: Correct: poor cash management is one of the leading causes of failure.

options.content: Having loyal customers who return often
options.rationale: Loyal customers support success.

options.content: Selling a product of high quality at a fair price
options.rationale: Quality and fair pricing help a business.

options.content: Having a clear and realistic business plan
options.rationale: Sound planning reduces the risk of failure.

explanation: A business that cannot pay its bills when due fails even if sales are rising.

stem: What is **liquidation**?

options.content: Closing a firm and selling assets to pay debts
options.rationale: Correct: the assets are sold and creditors are paid from the proceeds.

options.content: Selling extra shares to raise new finance for growth
options.rationale: That is raising capital, not closing the business.

options.content: Merging with a competitor to grow larger
options.rationale: A merger is external growth.

options.content: Moving production to a cheaper site
options.rationale: Relocation keeps the business running.

explanation: Liquidation ends the business by selling its assets to pay creditors.

stem: Which action would help a business **reduce the risk of failure**?

options.content: Expanding into new markets without research
options.rationale: Expansion without research raises risk.

options.content: Ignoring competitors' price changes
options.rationale: Ignoring rivals can lose customers.

options.content: Delaying payment of all wages to save cash
options.rationale: This would damage workers' morale and could breach labour rules.

options.content: Preparing a cash flow forecast each month
options.rationale: Correct: forecasting shows cash shortages early so action can be taken.

explanation: Cash flow control and planning are standard ways of reducing the risk of failure.

stem: Why can a profitable business still fail?

options.content: Profit always falls once sales begin to rise
options.rationale: Rising sales normally raise profit unless costs rise faster.

options.content: It may be unable to pay bills on time
options.rationale: Correct: profit is not the same as cash available to pay debts.

options.content: Profit is always paid out in full as tax
options.rationale: Tax takes only a share of profit.

options.content: Profitable businesses never need suppliers
options.rationale: All businesses need suppliers.

explanation: Customers may pay late while suppliers and wages must be paid on time, causing a cash shortage.

stem: A fictional hardware shop in Mutare borrowed heavily to open three new branches in one year, before its first shop had proved profitable. Sales at the new branches were lower than forecast and loan repayments could not be met. Which cause of failure is shown?

options.content: Lack of competition
options.rationale: Nothing in the case concerns competition.

options.content: Over-staffing in the first shop
options.rationale: Staff numbers are not mentioned.

options.content: Excellent market research
options.rationale: Sales were lower than forecast, so the research was not sound.

options.content: Over-expansion of the business
options.rationale: Correct: the business grew faster than its finance and sales could support.

explanation: Opening too many outlets too quickly, financed by debt, is over-expansion.
hints: Which cause involves growing too fast?

stem: A bakery's owner finds that falling incomes in the town have reduced demand for bread. Which cause of failure does this illustrate?

options.content: Poor labour relations
options.rationale: Labour relations are not mentioned.

options.content: Weak product design
options.rationale: Product design is not the problem in the case.

options.content: A change in the economy
options.rationale: Correct: lower incomes are an economic change outside the owner's control.

options.content: Heavy over-borrowing
options.rationale: Borrowing is not mentioned.

explanation: Falling incomes are a change in the economy, an external cause of failure.
hints: Is the cause inside or outside the business?

stem: A fictional garage in Bulawayo has rising sales but has begun to pay suppliers late. Which analysis best explains why this may end in failure?

options.content: Suppliers will pay the garage more as sales rise
options.rationale: Suppliers are paid by the garage, not the other way.

options.content: Late payment always raises profit permanently
options.rationale: It can ease cash briefly but harms supplier trust.

options.content: Suppliers may refuse credit, so parts cannot be bought
options.rationale: Correct: loss of supplier trust cuts off inputs and sales.

options.content: Rising sales cannot cause cash problems
options.rationale: Fast growth often needs more cash for stock and wages.

explanation: Late payment damages trust; suppliers may demand cash on delivery or stop supplying, which interrupts production.
hints: What can suppliers do when they are paid late?

stem: Which is the best reason why a small business might decide NOT to spend heavily on market research before launching a product?

options.content: Market research always gives wrong answers to firms
options.rationale: Research can be accurate, though not perfect.

options.content: The cost may be too high for its cash flow
options.rationale: Correct: research is useful but costs money a small firm may lack.

options.content: Customers never change what they want to buy
options.rationale: Tastes do change.

options.content: Research increases the risk of failure
options.rationale: Research normally reduces risk.

explanation: Reducing risk has a cost; a small firm may prefer cheaper methods such as talking to customers.
hints: Compare the benefit of research with its cost.

stem: A business that makes a profit cannot fail.
explanation: False. A profitable business can fail if it runs out of cash to pay debts on time.

stem: When a company goes into administration, an independent administrator tries to keep it trading or to sell it as a going concern.
explanation: True. Administration aims to rescue the business or sell it; liquidation ends it.

stem: Match each cause of failure to the example.

right.content: A new licence fee the owner had not budgeted for
An owner who does not check stock or costs
A shop buys more stock than it can pay for
A new supermarket opens nearby and cuts prices

explanation: Each example matches the named cause.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

payload.template: {{blank:a}} means closing a business and selling its assets to pay creditors, whereas {{blank:b}} puts a struggling company under an independent administrator who tries to keep it trading.

explanation: Liquidation ends the business; administration tries to rescue it.

stem: A fictional hair salon in Gweru starts a month with US\$1,800 in the bank. During the month it receives US\$5,400 from customers and pays out US\$8,100 for wages, rent and supplies. By how much is the bank account overdrawn at the end of the month?
explanation: 1,800 + 5,400 − 8,100 = −900, an overdraft of US\$900. Using payments less receipts gives US\$2,700, which ignores opening cash.
workedSolution: 1. 1,800 + 5,400 − 8,100 = −900, an overdraft of US\$900. Using payments less receipts gives US\$2,700, which ignores opening cash.
hints: Add receipts to opening cash, then deduct payments.

stem: A fictional bakery in Chinhoyi has monthly sales of US\$18,500 and total costs of US\$14,300 (assume the costs do not change when sales change). A new competitor takes 15% of its sales. Calculate the percentage fall in the bakery's monthly profit, to one decimal place.
explanation: Profit before = 18,500 − 14,300 = 4,200. Sales after = 18,500 × 0.85 = 15,725, so profit after = 15,725 − 14,300 = 1,425. Fall = (4,200 − 1,425) ÷ 4,200 × 100 = 66.1%. A 15% sales fall causes a much larger fall in profit because costs stay the same.
workedSolution: 1. Profit before = 18,500 − 14,300 = 4,200. Sales after = 18,500 × 0.85 = 15,725, so profit after = 15,725 − 14,300 = 1,425. Fall = (4,200 − 1,425) ÷ 4,200 × 100 = 66.1%. A 15% sales fall causes a much larger fall in profit because costs stay the same.
hints: Work out the profit before and after the fall in sales.

stem: State **one** cause of business failure.
explanation: Accept poor cash management, over-expansion, weak management, competition, economic or legal change, or poor planning.

stem: Name the term for closing a company and selling its assets to pay its debts.
explanation: Liquidation is the closing down of the business and selling of assets to pay creditors.

stem: Explain why poor cash management is a common cause of business failure.

points.description: A business must pay suppliers, wages and rent when they fall due
Customers may pay late, so cash received can be less than cash due out
If bills cannot be paid, suppliers stop supplying and lenders may close the business, even if it is profitable

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A business has to pay suppliers, wages and rent on time. If customers pay late, cash coming in is less than cash going out. When bills cannot be paid, suppliers stop supplying and lenders may act, so the business can close even if it is profitable.

explanation: One point per mark.
hints: Think about timing: when money comes in and when it must go out.

stem: Moyo's Tuck Shop in Masvingo has lost customers since a larger shop opened across the road. Explain **two** ways in which the owner could reduce the risk of the business failing.

points.description: Conduct market research to find out what local customers want
Application: stock goods the larger shop does not, such as credit sales to regulars
Control cash flow by forecasting and keeping stock low
Application: avoid buying slow-selling goods that tie up money

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: He could carry out market research to find what his regulars want, then stock items the larger shop does not sell. He could also control cash flow with a simple forecast and buy only fast-selling goods, so that less money is tied up in unsold stock.

explanation: Two ways, each developed.
hints: Link each remedy to the tuck shop's situation.

stem: Analyse the consequences of the failure of a large clothing factory for the community of a small town.

points.description: Workers lose their jobs and incomes
Spending by households in local shops falls
Local businesses lose sales, and some may close
The town loses tax revenue, so public services may suffer

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Workers lose their jobs and so their incomes. They spend less in local shops, which lose sales and may have to lay off staff or close. The town also loses tax revenue from the factory and its workers, so there is less money for public services.

explanation: A chain of cause and effect.
hints: Follow the chain from jobs to spending to local business.

stem: A fictional business: Farai's Fresh Foods, in Mutare, supplies vegetables to three restaurants. Over six months it has expanded from one delivery van to four, financed by a bank loan. Two of the restaurants have now closed, and a third pays 90 days after delivery. Farai's cash balance at the end of the month was US\$600 against bills of US\$4,100 due next week.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the shortfall of cash against the bills due next week.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain **two** causes of the cash problem faced by Farai's Fresh Foods.

points.description: Over-expansion: four vans financed by loan raised costs and repayments
Loss of customers: two restaurants closed, reducing sales
Late-paying customer: 90 days' credit delays cash coming in

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Buying four vans increased the loan repayments and running costs before sales had grown. Two of his three customers closed, so sales fell, and the remaining one takes 90 days to pay, so cash comes in late.

parts.explanation: Any two causes with explanation; 3 marks for two developed causes.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Assess how Farai could reduce the risk of failure.

points.description: Chase the debt or ask for shorter credit terms from the slow-paying restaurant
Sell or lease out spare vans to cut costs
Find new customers through market research
Judgement: cash action first, as the bills are due next week

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: He should first collect cash from the slow-paying restaurant or negotiate a shorter payment period, because the bills are due next week. Selling or leasing spare vans would cut repayments. He should then research new customers to replace the closed restaurants. Cash must come first, because without it the business cannot survive to win new customers.

parts.explanation: Actions plus a judgement about priority.

explanation: Shortfall US\$3,500; causes are over-expansion, lost customers and late payment; actions are cash first.
hints: Subtract cash held from bills due.

stem: A fictional business: Nyasha's Photo Studio in Bulawayo made a profit of US\$6,000 last year but is struggling to pay its bills. It buys equipment on credit, sells most services on 30 days' credit and has no cash reserve. A friend suggests that it should reduce the risk of failure by diversifying into printing T-shirts.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain how a profitable business such as Nyasha's can still struggle to pay its bills.

points.description: Profit is not the same as cash
Customers pay after 30 days while the studio must pay equipment suppliers and costs sooner
With no cash reserve, any delay leaves the studio unable to pay on time

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Profit is not cash. Customers take 30 days to pay but the studio must pay its suppliers and costs sooner, and with no reserve any delay leaves it without cash to meet bills.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether diversifying into printing T-shirts is the best way for Nyasha to reduce the risk of failure.

points.description: Benefit: a second income source spreads risk
Cost: new equipment and stock need cash the studio does not have
Diversifying does not solve the cash timing problem
Alternative: better credit control, a cash flow forecast or a cash reserve
Condition: diversification suits a business that already has cash
Judgement and reason

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Printing T-shirts would give a second source of income, which spreads risk. But it needs new equipment and stock, which the studio cannot afford while it is short of cash, and it does not solve the delay in customer payments. Better credit control and a cash flow forecast would address the real problem at lower cost. Diversification may help later, once cash is under control.

parts.explanation: Weighs a suggestion against alternatives and reaches a reasoned judgement.
hints: Does the suggestion tackle the actual cause of the problem?

explanation: Cash timing is the cause; diversifying costs cash, so cash control comes first.
hints: Identify the true cause of the trouble first.
